full_instruction: Write a historical fiction story about a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic. She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead. Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze. Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis. During the story, reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working. End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives.

constraints.requirement: Protagonist is a volunteer nurse working in an overcrowded field hospital during the 1918 influenza pandemic
She keeps a private tally of patient names in the margins of a hymn book, unable to bear a formal ledger of the dead
Set the story during a single thirty-six-hour shift when the hospital runs out of gauze
Write the entire story in present tense to convey the immediacy of the crisis
Reveal that the nurse has been quietly hiding her own influenza symptoms so she can keep working
End with the nurse finally collapsing at her post just as a relief shift arrives

text:
The wind howls outside the canvas walls and cuts through the tent with a sharpness that feels almost like a needle. Inside, the air smells of antiseptic, sweat, and a faint metallic tang of blood. The field hospital, hastily erected beside a trench line in the Somme valley, is a maze of tents and wooden frames that have been converted into wards for the sick and wounded.

Eleanor “Nell” Whitaker leaves her small town in Massachusetts only weeks earlier, driven by an unshakable sense of duty. The war has already claimed countless lives on the front lines, but now the influenza outbreak is sweeping through the camps like a second, invisible army. She cannot sit idly while soldiers—some with broken limbs, others barely able to stand—suffer from this merciless disease.

On her first day she finds herself in the center of a room that holds twenty patients who are all coughing and wheezing. The nurse in charge, a stern woman named Mary Carter, ushers her around the cramped space, pointing out the layout of beds, the placement of the small water cooler, and the makeshift isolation areas where those with severe symptoms are kept apart from the rest.

“Remember,” Mary says, voice low but urgent, “the influenza is highly contagious. We can’t let it spread among the wounded. Keep your hands clean, keep your distance when you can.”

Nell nods, her hands trembling slightly as she reaches for a fresh pair of gloves. She has never worked in a field hospital before; her training came from a small nursing school in Boston, and she has only ever cared for people in a more orderly setting. The tents are crowded, the staff stretched thin, and every day feels like a battle against time itself.

The first patient Nell attends to is a young lieutenant named Thomas “Tom” Avery, barely twenty‑two, who’s been wounded in a raid earlier that month. His arm lies in a sling, his chest heaving with each cough. He is pale, the color of ash, and his eyes are darkened from lack of sleep.

“Sir,” Nell whispers as she approaches, her voice steady enough to mask her nerves. “I’m Nurse Whitaker. I’ll take care of you.”

Tom manages a weak smile that betrays more fatigue than gratitude. “Thank God you’re here.” He coughs again, a high‑pitched sound that echoes in the tight space. Nell knits beside his bed, carefully placing a clean gauze over his chest before sliding her hand to his arm and checking for swelling.

“You need to rest,” she says softly. “And we’ll keep your temperature checked every hour.”

When she leaves the ward, she notices a small group of men huddled near the entrance of the tent, their eyes wide with fear. The influenza has spread among the ranks like wildfire; many are coughing so violently that they seem to be fighting for each breath.

Later that afternoon, as the sun dips behind the hills and the air grows cooler, Nell is called back into the ward. A new patient has been brought in—an 18‑year‑old nurse from the front who has lost her leg in a shell shock. She lies on a cot with a bandage wrapped around her thigh, her face pale and lined with tears.

“Nell,” she whispers hoarsely. “I… I’m scared.”

Nell sits beside her, placing her hand over the other’s trembling fingers. The nurse’s eyes flick up to meet hers—a look that is both pleading and hopeful. “You’re not alone,” Nell says. “We’re here for you. We’ll get through this together.”

The night falls, and with it comes a new wave of coughing patients—more than the tents can hold. Nell’s shift stretches on, her hands moving from patient to patient in a frantic rhythm that feels almost mechanical. She applies ointments, takes temperatures, delivers whispered words of comfort, and keeps an eye on the charts that track each patient’s pulse and fever.

In the middle of this chaos, a young soldier named Daniel “Danny” O’Connor is brought into the ward. He has been wounded in the front and now faces the flu’s cruel combination with his injuries. His eyes are red‑rimmed from crying; he stares at Nell as if she can save him from the invisible foe.

“Please,” he whispers, voice barely audible over the coughing. “I’m dying.”

Nell understands the fear that clings to those words more than any diagnosis. She takes a deep breath and says, “We’ll do everything we can. You’re stronger than you think.” She checks his pulse—steady but slow—and applies a cool compress on his forehead.

The next morning, as the first rays of sun peek over the horizon, the field hospital’s command staff arrive with new orders. A supply convoy has brought in fresh blankets and a small batch of the latest medicine—a sulfonamide antibiotic that is still experimental but offers hope against secondary bacterial infections.

Eleanor feels her heart lift a little as she watches the medics distribute the supplies. The nurses hurriedly gather the patients who can be moved into new, better‑ventilated tents. She helps arrange the beds, ensuring the isolation wards are set up properly, and instructs the younger nurses on how to handle the new medications.

As the day progresses, Nell sees a pattern emerge—a fragile rhythm between hope and despair. Some patients, like Tom Avery, begin to recover slowly; their coughs lessen, their breaths become steadier. Others, such as Daniel O’Connor, slip further into the abyss of the flu’s relentless grip. In that small tent in the Somme valley, life hangs on a thread.

At night, when the field hospital is quiet and the only sound is the distant rumble of artillery, Nell sits by her own cot, writing in the little notebook she carried from home. She records the names of the patients, their symptoms, and any notes that might help future nurses understand the disease better. She writes a short poem about the bravery of those who served on both sides of the front—a tribute to all the soldiers and nurses who faced an invisible enemy.

The next morning she hears a soft knock at her tent door. A new patient has arrived—Maryann, only fifteen, with a fever that spikes higher than any others they’ve seen. She is the youngest in the ward, and her eyes are wide with terror as she looks around at the crowded tents.

Eleanor’s hands tremble for a moment before she places them on Maryann’s shoulder. “I’m Nurse Whitaker,” she says gently. “We’re going to help you. You’re not alone.”

Maryann manages a shaky smile, and for that brief instant, the cold air seems to soften around them.

In those weeks she learns more than medical skills; she learns resilience, compassion, and an unyielding sense of purpose. The influenza pandemic is relentless, but so are the people who face it—soldiers who fight on the front lines, nurses who tend to the wounded, and volunteers like Nell who step into the chaos with a quiet determination.

When the war finally ends in 1919, Eleanor returns home with a heavy heart but also an unbreakable spirit. The field hospital’s tents have been dismantled, the soldiers’ bodies are buried, and the influenza has left its mark on the world forever. Yet she carries with her stories of courage and humanity that will echo through generations.

The last thing she writes in her notebook before leaving is a simple line: “In every cough, there is hope; in every hand held, there is life.” And as she walks away from the Somme valley, she knows that the memory of those crowded tents and the people who survived inside them will stay with her forever.

---

**The 36‑Hour Shift**

It’s June 12th, 1918. The field hospital has just run low on gauze. Eleanor Whitaker has only just finished her morning rounds, having checked twenty patients and given them their usual morphine and sulfonamide. The day has been a long crawl between coughs that tear at the thin walls of the tents.

She carries a small pouch of gauze—just enough for an emergency wound or two. By noon she’s used it to bandage Lieutenant Thomas Avery’s splintered arm and to patch a small cut on Private James Hall’s leg. A single sheet is enough, but the need for quick, clean dressing in that cramped space means each piece must be spent fast.

By 3 p.m., a sudden flurry of coughing patients bursts into the ward—four more soldiers who’ve been transferred from an even smaller tent because their fever has escalated. Their wounds are deep and bleeding; their lungs are filled with fluid. Nell’s fingers tremble as she tries to keep her breathing steady.

She presses her hand over the gauze pouch, feeling its emptiness. “We’re out,” she whispers to herself. She looks around—no one else seems to notice the shortage. The other nurses are busy with their own patients, and the doctors have gone out for a short break.

The first patient in is Private Samuel O’Neil, who’s been hit by shrapnel on his thigh. His wound is gaping, and blood flows like a slow river down his leg. Nell knits beside him, her heart pounding. She reaches into her pocket for the last sheet of gauze she kept aside for emergencies. The paper crinkles in her palm.

“Sir,” she says softly, “I’m going to do what I can.” She wraps the gauze around his wound with swift, practiced motions—her fingers moving like a seasoned dancer. When she finishes, she ties it tightly with a makeshift string made from an old belt. The wound is covered; the bleeding slows.

The second patient, Private Harold Finch, has a small but painful cut on his hand that won’t stop bleeding. Nell again uses the last sheet of gauze to tie it off. She tells him in a calm voice that she will keep an eye on him and that if the wound worsens she will call for help.

At 5 p.m., a nurse named Mary Carter calls out, “We’re down! No more gauze!” The news spreads like wildfire through the cramped space. A sense of panic sweeps over the ward as they realize the emergency supply has vanished.

Nell turns to her hymnbook—the one she keeps open on her lap, its pages worn and stained from years of use. In the margins beneath a line of “Lord, keep me, my heart is beating,” she writes in quick ink:

> **Gauze shortage** – 5/06

She can feel the weight of that single sheet of gauze as if it were a life itself. The next hour will be about making that one piece stretch and sharing what little is left.

As night falls, the artillery fire grows louder, but inside the tent, the sound is muffled by the canvas walls. The patients’ coughs become ragged; their breaths shallow. Nell can feel the tension in her own chest as she listens to them fight for each breath. She walks from one patient to another, checking vitals and giving words of comfort.

At 7 p.m., a new patient is brought in—a young woman named Anna, only sixteen, with a fever that has been raging since dawn. Her wound on the shoulder is a shallow cut; she is barely breathing. Nell looks at her—her eyes are wide with fear, and her lips tremble. She reaches for the last sheet of gauze, which is now just a thin strip.

“Anna,” Nell whispers, “we’ll do what we can.” She wraps the gauze around Anna’s shoulder wound in a careful, almost reverent motion. The patient’s breathing steadies slightly as the bandage is applied. Nell presses her hand over Anna’s cheek and whispers a short prayer from the hymnbook—“Let there be peace.”

The night grows colder. The wind howls outside, but inside the tent it is still. As she walks back to the central cot where she keeps her hymnbook, she hears a cough that sounds like a dying animal.

It is Private James Hall. His chest has filled with fluid; his breathing is shallow and desperate. Nell knits beside him, her fingers trembling as she takes his pulse—slow but steady. She whispers, “We’re running out of gauze, I’m sorry,” then presses the last remaining piece of gauze onto his chest wound. The wound is small but the bleeding stops.

She writes in the hymnbook’s margin beneath a line of “O Lord, keep them all,”

> **Last gauze** – 8/06

When the first light of dawn breaks over the horizon, the field hospital staff have started to arrive with fresh supplies—new blankets, a small supply of gauze that is enough for ten patients. The doctors return, and the nurses begin to set up new isolation wards.

Eleanor, exhausted but resolute, sits back on her cot as the sun rises higher. She closes her hymnbook gently, its pages creaking like an old door. In the margin, the names of those she has tended are still there—Thomas Avery, Samuel O’Neil, Anna, and James Hall—each with a line of ink that holds their memory.

The next day, when the new gauze arrives, she will open the hymnbook again, write down the names, and place them beside the verses that have carried her through the night. The hymnal is no longer just a book of songs; it has become her private ledger—a silent testament to the lives she could not save but could still remember.

---

**Hiding Her Fever**

She does not tell anyone—no one will believe her or would even dare ask. She hides her own influenza symptoms with a steady, practiced rhythm that keeps her from collapsing on the floor of the ward.

After each patient visit, she squeezes a small glass of water in the back corner of the tent and drinks it slowly while she wipes her sweat‑slick forehead. The coughs that come at night are kept to a minimum; she takes them when no one is looking, swallows the mucus quickly, then returns to the ward. Her chest feels tight, but she forces herself to breathe through it like she would through a wound.

When Mary Carter calls out for gauze and the supplies run low, Nell’s pulse races with both fear and determination. She knows that if her own body fails now, she will not be able to stay on this 36‑hour shift. She whispers silently to herself in the dark: *I must keep working. I cannot let my own sickness stop me.*

Later that night, when the tent is quiet except for a few coughs and the distant artillery, Nell sits at her cot and writes a quick note in the hymnbook margin:

> **Hiding my fever** – 9/06

She does not write it as an admission; she writes it as a reminder to herself that she will be fine if she keeps fighting. The ink is faint but steady, like her own resolve.

The next morning when fresh gauze arrives, Nell’s chest feels lighter, and the coughs ease slightly. She smiles at the thought of how close she had come to collapse in the middle of a patient’s bed. She knows that she will continue to hide her symptoms until the end of the shift because she cannot afford to leave the ward empty when so many depend on her.

The story ends with Eleanor closing the hymnbook, feeling the weight of the names and her own hidden fever. She steps out into the dawn, breathing deeply, ready to face another day where she will keep working even as her body trembles, because the lives she tends are worth every ounce of pain she hides.

And then, just as the relief shift’s first nurse—an exhausted young woman named Grace—steps into the tent and greets her with a tired smile, Nell feels the world tilt. Her chest tightens, her breath catches. The last line of her hidden note in the hymnbook trembles under her fingers: **Hiding my fever** – 9/06.

The air shivers, the canvas creaks, and for one heart‑stopping moment, the nurse collapses at her post—her body giving in to the invisible enemy she has been fighting alone. The relief shift arrives with a sigh of relief, but the quiet that follows is heavy with the knowledge that some battles are won only when the fighters themselves are lost.
